selected_themes: Buyer expectations diverge: private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025; geographically, private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, while dealmakers outside the US, particularly corporates, face greater uncertainty. These are expectations and qualitative comparisons, not realized activity or quantified geographic measures.

For the estimated value of the next M&A transaction, displayed size-band percentages sum to below US$1B for 81% of corporate estimates and 94% of private-equity estimates; the largest individual band is US$250M to <US$500M at 32% and 50%, respectively. These are estimates, not completed transactions, and the report describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

Deal types under consideration show the sharpest stated buyer difference in carve-outs: 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference; acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% and 69%, respectively. These chart values describe deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

The report’s deal-execution discussion presents AI’s contribution as expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing work: new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of prior cost. Its customer-concentration diligence example assigns execution to an agent and review and decisions to a human; neither claim is a measured outcome.

A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness and gaps visible before close; the report says surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning rather than after close reduces tolerance for execution failures. This is a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.

The report records an early-2026 decline of nearly $1 trillion in market value for software and knowledge-services stocks over a matter of weeks. It says the repricing was not driven by collapsing revenues: many affected companies reported stable or growing earnings, while the market’s multiple for future cash flows changed.

The distinction matters for planning: stronger private-equity pipeline expectations do not establish that next deals will be larger, while the report describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

evidence_spans.text: The page’s narrative explicitly identifies the survey population as private-equity dealmakers and says they are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025. The following paragraph contrasts corporates’ more measured outlook and says fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. Both assertions are framed as expectations; the page does not claim these outcomes have been realized.

The “Geography amplifies the divergence” section directly gives the claimed relationship: private equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure. The page supports this as a qualitative comparison, not a quantified measure.

selected_themes: Buyer expectations diverge: private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025; geographically, private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, while dealmakers outside the US, particularly corporates, face greater uncertainty. These are expectations and qualitative comparisons, not realized activity or quantified geographic measures.

For the estimated value of the next M&A transaction, displayed size-band percentages sum to below US$1B for 81% of corporate estimates and 94% of private-equity estimates; the largest individual band is US$250M to <US$500M at 32% and 50%, respectively. These are estimates, not completed transactions, and the report describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

Deal types under consideration show the sharpest stated buyer difference in carve-outs: 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference; acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% and 69%, respectively. These chart values describe deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

The report’s deal-execution discussion presents AI’s contribution as expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing work: new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of prior cost. Its customer-concentration diligence example assigns execution to an agent and review and decisions to a human; neither claim is a measured outcome.

A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness and gaps visible before close; the report says surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning rather than after close reduces tolerance for execution failures. This is a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.

The report records an early-2026 decline of nearly $1 trillion in market value for software and knowledge-services stocks over a matter of weeks. claim_ledgers.claim_text: Compared with corporates, private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase versus 2025.
Across displayed size bands for estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the below-US$1B bands total 81% for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates.
For deal types under consideration, carve-out acquisitions are displayed at 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference.

The report says organizations are sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.
In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI expands analysis by making new categories of analysis worth doing, rather than merely accelerating existing analysis.

Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025; corporates have a more measured outlook, and fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. These are expectations, not realized activity. Separately, the report says private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

For the estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the displayed percentage bands below US$1B sum to 81% for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates. The largest individual band for both buyer types is US$250M to <US$500M, at 32% for corporate estimates and 50% for private-equity estimates. The page describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

For carve-out acquisitions under consideration, the chart displays 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed difference of +34 percentage points in favor of Private equity. Acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% for Corporate and 69% for Private equity. Both categories are deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report identifies “Strategic focus in a fragmented world” as one of five drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment. It describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI’s advantage is expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing analysis: entirely new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of the prior cost. In its customer-concentration diligence example, an agent ingests and segments customer data, models concentration risk under multiple scenarios, compares against sector benchmarks, drafts the relevant report section, and flags anomalies; the human reviews and decides while the agent executes.

A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness and gaps visible before close. The report says surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning, rather than discovering them after close, reduces tolerance for execution failures.

In early 2026, software and knowledge-services stocks lost nearly $1 trillion in market value over a matter of weeks. The report says the repricing was not driven by collapsing revenues: many affected companies reported stable or growing earnings, while the market’s multiple for future cash flows changed.

editorial_plan.report_thesis: The 2026 M&A outlook combines stronger pipeline expectations among private-equity dealmakers than corporates with next-transaction estimates concentrated below US$1B, while the report emphasizes portfolio focus and broader, earlier deal-execution analysis.

themes.theme: Buyer expectations diverge: private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025; geographically, private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, while dealmakers outside the US, particularly corporates, face greater uncertainty. These are expectations and qualitative comparisons, not realized activity or quantified geographic measures.

For the estimated value of the next M&A transaction, displayed size-band percentages sum to below US$1B for 81% of corporate estimates and 94% of private-equity estimates; the largest individual band is US$250M to <US$500M at 32% and 50%, respectively. These are estimates, not completed transactions, and the report describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

Deal types under consideration show the sharpest stated buyer difference in carve-outs: 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference; acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% and 69%, respectively. These chart values describe deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

The report’s deal-execution discussion presents AI’s contribution as expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing work: new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of prior cost. Its customer-concentration diligence example assigns execution to an agent and review and decisions to a human; neither claim is a measured outcome.

A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness and gaps visible before close; the report says surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning rather than after close reduces tolerance for execution failures. This is a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.

insights_final.so_what: Pipeline expectations differ by buyer type, while the report describes geographic differences qualitatively rather than as quantified measures.
insights_final.text: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025; corporates have a more measured outlook, and fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. These are expectations, not realized activity. Separately, the report says private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

artifacts_payload.linkedin_post:
Private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025. Corporates have a more measured outlook, and fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. These are expectations, not realized activity.

Geographically, private-equity optimism is strongest in the US. Outside the US, dealmakers, particularly corporates, face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

MarketLense recommends segmenting pipeline scenarios by buyer type and location, while distinguishing expectations from realized activity.

summary.executive_summary: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025. Across displayed size bands for estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the below-US$1B bands total 81% for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates. For deal types under consideration, carve-out acquisitions are displayed at 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference. The report says organizations are sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment. In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI expands analysis by making new categories of analysis worth doing, rather than merely accelerating existing analysis.
summary.tldr: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025.

source_truth_notes_by_page.16: The “Geography amplifies the divergence” section directly gives the claimed relationship: private equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure. Outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

source_truth_notes_by_page.15: The page’s narrative explicitly identifies the survey population as private-equity dealmakers and says they are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025. The following paragraph contrasts corporates’ more measured outlook and says fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. Both assertions are framed as expectations; the page does not claim these outcomes have been realized.

qualifiers: The claims are presented as survey expectations, not realized M&A activity.
The comparison is between private-equity dealmakers and corporates; the page does not specify a geography or sample size for these statements.
verified_facts.statement: The report says survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025. By contrast, corporates have a more measured outlook: while many expect to remain active, fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. These are expectations, not realized activity.

source_truth_notes_by_page.17: The chart title identifies the subject as deal types under consideration and its columns are headed Corporate and Private equity. On the exact “Carve-out acquisitions” row, the displayed values are 21% and 55%, respectively, and the adjacent displayed difference is +34 pts. verified_facts.statement: For types of deals under consideration, the chart displays carve-out acquisitions at 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed difference of +34 percentage points in favor of Private equity.

source_truth_notes_by_page.9: The page heading identifies five drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment. The first driver is labeled “Strategic focus in a fragmented world,” and its text describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment. These statements support the corrected claim.

qualifiers: This is a qualitative statement about a driver of the 2026 M&A environment, not a quantified finding.
The report describes organizations generally and does not specify a narrower population, denominator, or geography for this driver.
verified_facts.statement: The report identifies strategic focus in a fragmented world as one of five drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment. It says organizations are sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

source_truth_notes_by_page.26: The deal-execution discussion explicitly contrasts expansion with acceleration: it says the significant effect is not that existing analysis gets faster, but that entirely new categories become worth doing. It also says previously uneconomical analysis at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of prior cost. The page presents these as qualitative claims and gives no numerical cost fraction.

qualifiers: This is the page’s qualitative argument, not a quantified measured result.
The page does not specify the amount of the cost reduction, a timeframe, or a geography.
verified_facts.statement: In its discussion of deal execution, the page argues that AI’s advantage is expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing analysis: entirely new categories of analysis become worth doing, and work previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of the prior cost.

source_truth_notes_by_page.28: The left column directly describes AI making execution readiness—and execution gaps—visible before close, and states that surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning rather than discovering them post-close reduces tolerance for execution failures. The page frames this as a qualitative finding about organizations, without a numerical measure.

qualifiers: The page presents this as a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.
The finding concerns execution readiness and gaps in the context of diligence and pre-close planning.
verified_facts.statement: A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness visible before close, making execution gaps visible as well. When risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers are surfaced during diligence and pre-close planning rather than discovered after close, tolerance for execution failures declines.

source_truth_notes_by_page.16: The chart titled “Estimated total deal value of next M&A transaction — corporate vs. private equity” explicitly labels the buyer-type columns and size bands. The three displayed bands below US$1B sum to 81% for corporate (20% + 32% + 29%) and 94% for private equity (11% + 50% + 33%). The US$250M to <US$500M band is 32% for corporate and 50% for private equity, the largest single band in each column. The accompanying text characterizes expectations as measured and says the anticipated rebound is led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals. The figures are estimates for the next transaction; the page does not specify a sample size, calendar period, or geography.

verified_facts.statement: Deal-size expectations are described as disciplined. For the estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the displayed size-band percentages sum to 81% below US$1B for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates. The largest individual band is US$250M to <US$500M, at 32% for corporate and 50% for private equity. The page describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

source_truth_notes_by_page.16: The “Geography amplifies the divergence” section directly gives the claimed relationship: private equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure. The page supports this as a qualitative comparison, not a quantified measure.

qualifiers: The source describes relative risk appetite and uncertainty qualitatively; it gives no numerical measure for these statements.
The greater uncertainty outside the US is stated for dealmakers, with corporates singled out in particular.
verified_facts.statement: Geography reinforces differences in buyer risk appetite: private equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure remain comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility. Outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

source_truth_notes_by_page.26: The right-hand column gives the customer-concentration diligence example and lists the workflow steps: ingesting raw data, segmenting by customer, modeling under multiple scenarios, comparing against sector benchmarks, drafting the relevant diligence-report section, and flagging anomalies for the deal team. It expressly says the human reviews and decides while the agent executes.

qualifiers: The example concerns diligence on a target’s customer concentration.
The page describes the agent’s workflow and the human’s review and decision role; it does not report a measured outcome.
verified_facts.statement: In the page’s customer-concentration diligence example, an agent ingests raw data, segments customers, models concentration risk under multiple scenarios, compares against sector benchmarks, drafts the relevant section of the diligence report, and flags anomalies for the deal team’s attention; the human reviews and decides, while the agent executes.

selected_themes: Buyer expectations diverge: private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025; geographically, private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, while dealmakers outside the US, particularly corporates, face greater uncertainty. These are expectations and qualitative comparisons, not realized activity or quantified geographic measures.

For the estimated value of the next M&A transaction, displayed size-band percentages sum to below US$1B for 81% of corporate estimates and 94% of private-equity estimates; the largest individual band is US$250M to <US$500M at 32% and 50%, respectively. These are estimates, not completed transactions, and the report describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

Deal types under consideration show the sharpest stated buyer difference in carve-outs: 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference; acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% and 69%, respectively. These chart values describe deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

The report’s deal-execution discussion presents AI’s contribution as expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing work: new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of prior cost. Its customer-concentration diligence example assigns execution to an agent and review and decisions to a human; neither claim is a measured outcome.

A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness and gaps visible before close; the report says surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning rather than after close reduces tolerance for execution failures. This is a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.

The report records an early-2026 decline of nearly $1 trillion in market value for software and knowledge-services stocks over a matter of weeks. It says the repricing was not driven by collapsing revenues: many affected companies reported stable or growing earnings, while the market’s multiple for future cash flows changed.

public_output.executive_summary: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025. Across displayed size bands for estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the below-US$1B bands total 81% for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates. For deal types under consideration, carve-out acquisitions are displayed at 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference. The report says organizations are sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment. In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI expands analysis by making new categories of analysis worth doing, rather than merely accelerating existing analysis.
public_output.tldr: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025.

selected_themes: Buyer expectations diverge: private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025; geographically, private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, while dealmakers outside the US, particularly corporates, face greater uncertainty. These are expectations and qualitative comparisons, not realized activity or quantified geographic measures.

For the estimated value of the next M&A transaction, displayed size-band percentages sum to below US$1B for 81% of corporate estimates and 94% of private-equity estimates; the largest individual band is US$250M to <US$500M at 32% and 50%, respectively. These are estimates, not completed transactions, and the report describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

Deal types under consideration show the sharpest stated buyer difference in carve-outs: 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference; acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% and 69%, respectively. These chart values describe deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

The report’s deal-execution discussion presents AI’s contribution as expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing work: new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of prior cost. Its customer-concentration diligence example assigns execution to an agent and review and decisions to a human; neither claim is a measured outcome.

A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness and gaps visible before close; the report says surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning rather than after close reduces tolerance for execution failures. This is a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.

The report records an early-2026 decline of nearly $1 trillion in market value for software and knowledge-services stocks over a matter of weeks. It says the repricing was not driven by collapsing revenues: many affected companies reported stable or growing earnings, while the market’s multiple for future cash flows changed.

claim_ledgers.claim_text: Compared with corporates, private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase versus 2025.
Across displayed size bands for estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the below-US$1B bands total 81% for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates.
For deal types under consideration, carve-out acquisitions are displayed at 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference.

The report says organizations are sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.
In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI expands analysis by making new categories of analysis worth doing, rather than merely accelerating existing analysis.

Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025; corporates have a more measured outlook, and fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. These are expectations, not realized activity. Separately, the report says private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

For the estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the displayed percentage bands below US$1B sum to 81% for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates. The largest individual band for both buyer types is US$250M to <US$500M, at 32% for corporate estimates and 50% for private-equity estimates. The page describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

For carve-out acquisitions under consideration, the chart displays 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed difference of +34 percentage points in favor of Private equity. Acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% for Corporate and 69% for Private equity. Both categories are deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report identifies “Strategic focus in a fragmented world” as one of five drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment. It describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI’s advantage is expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing analysis: entirely new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of the prior cost. In its customer-concentration diligence example, an agent ingests and segments customer data, models concentration risk under multiple scenarios, compares against sector benchmarks, drafts the relevant report section, and flags anomalies; the human reviews and decides while the agent executes.

A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness and gaps visible before close. The report says surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning, rather than discovering them after close, reduces tolerance for execution failures.

In early 2026, software and knowledge-services stocks lost nearly $1 trillion in market value over a matter of weeks. The report says the repricing was not driven by collapsing revenues: many affected companies reported stable or growing earnings, while the market’s multiple for future cash flows changed.

themes.theme: Buyer expectations diverge: private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025; geographically, private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, while dealmakers outside the US, particularly corporates, face greater uncertainty. Deal types under consideration show the sharpest stated buyer difference in carve-outs: 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference; acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% and 69%, respectively. These chart values describe deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

This is a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.

The three displayed bands below US$1B sum to 81% for corporate (20% + 32% + 29%) and 94% for private equity (11% + 50% + 33%). The US$250M to <US$500M band is 32% for corporate and 50% for private equity, the largest single band in each column. The accompanying text characterizes expectations as measured and says the anticipated rebound is led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals. The figures are estimates for the next transaction; the page does not specify a sample size, calendar period, or geography.

The page describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

insights_final.text: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025; corporates have a more measured outlook, and fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. insights_final.text: In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI’s advantage is expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing analysis: entirely new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of the prior cost. In its customer-concentration diligence example, an agent ingests and segments customer data, models concentration risk under multiple scenarios, compares against sector benchmarks, drafts the relevant report section, and flags anomalies; the human reviews and decides while the agent executes.

Private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025. Corporates have a more measured outlook, and fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. These are expectations, not realized activity.

Geographically, private-equity optimism is strongest in the US. Outside the US, dealmakers, particularly corporates, face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

MarketLense recommends segmenting pipeline scenarios by buyer type and location, while distinguishing expectations from realized activity.

summary.executive_summary: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025. Across displayed size bands for estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the below-US$1B bands total 81% for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates. For deal types under consideration, carve-out acquisitions are displayed at 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed +34 percentage-point difference. The report says organizations are sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment. In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI expands analysis by making new categories of analysis worth doing, rather than merely accelerating existing analysis.
summary.tldr: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely than corporates to expect M&A pipeline activity to increase relative to 2025.

The following paragraph contrasts corporates’ more measured outlook and says fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. Both assertions are framed as expectations; the page does not claim these outcomes have been realized.

qualifiers: The claims are presented as survey expectations, not realized M&A activity.
The comparison is between private-equity dealmakers and corporates; the page does not specify a geography or sample size for these statements.
verified_facts.statement: The report says survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025. By contrast, corporates have a more measured outlook: while many expect to remain active, fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. These are expectations, not realized activity.

source_truth_notes_by_page.26: The deal-execution discussion explicitly contrasts expansion with acceleration: it says the significant effect is not that existing analysis gets faster, but that entirely new categories become worth doing. It also says previously uneconomical analysis at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of prior cost. The page presents these as qualitative claims and gives no numerical cost fraction.

qualifiers: This is the page’s qualitative argument, not a quantified measured result.
The page does not specify the amount of the cost reduction, a timeframe, or a geography.
verified_facts.statement: In its discussion of deal execution, the page argues that AI’s advantage is expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing analysis: entirely new categories of analysis become worth doing, and work previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of the prior cost.

source_truth_notes_by_page.28: The left column directly describes AI making execution readiness—and execution gaps—visible before close, and states that surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning rather than discovering them post-close reduces tolerance for execution failures. The page frames this as a qualitative finding about organizations, without a numerical measure.

qualifiers: The page presents this as a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.
The finding concerns execution readiness and gaps in the context of diligence and pre-close planning.
verified_facts.statement: A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness visible before close, making execution gaps visible as well. When risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers are surfaced during diligence and pre-close planning rather than discovered after close, tolerance for execution failures declines.

source_truth_notes_by_page.16: The chart titled “Estimated total deal value of next M&A transaction — corporate vs. private equity” explicitly labels the buyer-type columns and size bands. The three displayed bands below US$1B sum to 81% for corporate (20% + 32% + 29%) and 94% for private equity (11% + 50% + 33%). The US$250M to <US$500M band is 32% for corporate and 50% for private equity, the largest single band in each column. The accompanying text characterizes expectations as measured and says the anticipated rebound is led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals. The figures are estimates for the next transaction; the page does not specify a sample size, calendar period, or geography.

verified_facts.statement: Deal-size expectations are described as disciplined. For the estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the displayed size-band percentages sum to 81% below US$1B for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates. The largest individual band is US$250M to <US$500M, at 32% for corporate and 50% for private equity. The page describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

source_truth_notes_by_page.16: The “Geography amplifies the divergence” section directly gives the claimed relationship: private equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure. The page supports this as a qualitative comparison, not a quantified measure.

qualifiers: The source describes relative risk appetite and uncertainty qualitatively; it gives no numerical measure for these statements.
The greater uncertainty outside the US is stated for dealmakers, with corporates singled out in particular.
verified_facts.statement: Geography reinforces differences in buyer risk appetite: private equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure remain comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility. Outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

source_truth_notes_by_page.26: The right-hand column gives the customer-concentration diligence example and lists the workflow steps: ingesting raw data, segmenting by customer, modeling under multiple scenarios, comparing against sector benchmarks, drafting the relevant diligence-report section, and flagging anomalies for the deal team. It expressly says the human reviews and decides while the agent executes.

qualifiers: The example concerns diligence on a target’s customer concentration.
The page describes the agent’s workflow and the human’s review and decision role; it does not report a measured outcome.
verified_facts.statement: In the page’s customer-concentration diligence example, an agent ingests raw data, segments customers, models concentration risk under multiple scenarios, compares against sector benchmarks, drafts the relevant section of the diligence report, and flags anomalies for the deal team’s attention; the human reviews and decides, while the agent executes.

These are expectations, not realized activity. Separately, the report says private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

The largest individual band for both buyer types is US$250M to <US$500M, at 32% for corporate estimates and 50% for private-equity estimates. The page describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

The report identifies “Strategic focus in a fragmented world” as one of five drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment. It describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI’s advantage is expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing analysis: entirely new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of the prior cost. In its customer-concentration diligence example, an agent ingests and segments customer data, models concentration risk under multiple scenarios, compares against sector benchmarks, drafts the relevant report section, and flags anomalies; the human reviews and decides while the agent executes.

insights: Survey results show private-equity dealmakers are significantly more likely to expect an increase in M&A pipeline activity relative to 2025; corporates have a more measured outlook, and fewer anticipate a material acceleration in deal volume. These are expectations, not realized activity. Separately, the report says private-equity optimism is strongest in the US, where capital availability and transaction infrastructure are comparatively supportive despite broader global volatility; outside the US, dealmakers—particularly corporates—face greater uncertainty related to growth, regulation and geopolitical exposure.

For the estimated total deal value of the next M&A transaction, the displayed percentage bands below US$1B sum to 81% for corporate estimates and 94% for private-equity estimates. The largest individual band for both buyer types is US$250M to <US$500M, at 32% for corporate estimates and 50% for private-equity estimates. The page describes the anticipated rebound as led by mid-sized, execution-intensive deals rather than megadeals.

For carve-out acquisitions under consideration, the chart displays 21% for Corporate and 55% for Private equity, with a displayed difference of +34 percentage points in favor of Private equity. Acquisition of a full business is listed at 62% for Corporate and 69% for Private equity. Both categories are deals under consideration, not completed transactions.

The report identifies “Strategic focus in a fragmented world” as one of five drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment. It describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

In its deal-execution discussion, the report argues that AI’s advantage is expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing analysis: entirely new categories become worth doing, and analysis previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of the prior cost. In its customer-concentration diligence example, an agent ingests and segments customer data, models concentration risk under multiple scenarios, compares against sector benchmarks, drafts the relevant report section, and flags anomalies; the human reviews and decides while the agent executes.

source_truth_notes_by_page.9: The page heading identifies five drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment. The first driver is labeled “Strategic focus in a fragmented world,” and its text describes organizations sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment. These statements support the corrected claim.

qualifiers: This is a qualitative statement about a driver of the 2026 M&A environment, not a quantified finding.
The report describes organizations generally and does not specify a narrower population, denominator, or geography for this driver.
verified_facts.statement: The report identifies strategic focus in a fragmented world as one of five drivers shaping the 2026 M&A environment. It says organizations are sharpening portfolio focus to concentrate capital, capabilities, and management attention where they believe they can build durable advantage in a more complex global environment.

source_truth_notes_by_page.26: The deal-execution discussion explicitly contrasts expansion with acceleration: it says the significant effect is not that existing analysis gets faster, but that entirely new categories become worth doing. It also says previously uneconomical analysis at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of prior cost. The page presents these as qualitative claims and gives no numerical cost fraction.

qualifiers: This is the page’s qualitative argument, not a quantified measured result.
The page does not specify the amount of the cost reduction, a timeframe, or a geography.
verified_facts.statement: In its discussion of deal execution, the page argues that AI’s advantage is expanding analysis, not merely accelerating existing analysis: entirely new categories of analysis become worth doing, and work previously uneconomical at traditional analyst-day rates becomes viable at a fraction of the prior cost.

source_truth_notes_by_page.28: The left column directly describes AI making execution readiness—and execution gaps—visible before close, and states that surfacing risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers during diligence and pre-close planning rather than discovering them post-close reduces tolerance for execution failures. The page frames this as a qualitative finding about organizations, without a numerical measure.

qualifiers: The page presents this as a qualitative finding, not a quantified rate or measured causal effect.
The finding concerns execution readiness and gaps in the context of diligence and pre-close planning.
verified_facts.statement: A growing number of organizations are finding that AI makes execution readiness visible before close, making execution gaps visible as well. When risks, dependencies, and value-creation levers are surfaced during diligence and pre-close planning rather than discovered after close, tolerance for execution failures declines.

Execution capability has become the 
defining factor in M&A outcomes.
Over successive deal cycles, evidence has shown that M&A 
outcomes are shaped as much by execution capability as by 
strategic intent. The conditions confronting dealmakers today 
suggest that this relationship is becoming even more 
pronounced.
The 2026 M&A environment is accelerating this reality. 
Dealmakers are operating amid geopolitical fragmentation, 
legislative and regulatory volatility, accelerating technological 
change, and intensifying pressure to focus capital and 
leadership attention where advantage can be sustained. 
Portfolio separation activity, including carve-outs, divestitures 
and staged ownership structures, is no longer a byproduct of 
other strategic choices. It has become a structural 
mechanism for reshaping portfolios in response to a more 
dynamic and less durable external environment.
What distinguishes the current environment is not that 
transactions are more complex than in prior cycles — 
complexity has always been present — but that the drivers of 
carve-out activity are increasingly structural. Rising risk 
concentration in non-core portfolio “tails,” shifting trade and 
tax regimes and accelerating capability reconfiguration are 
prompting boards to act more decisively and more 
persistently.
At the same time, advances in analytics and artificial 
intelligence are reshaping how deals are sourced, evaluated 
and executed. While technology alone does not determine 
outcomes, its integration into decision-making and execution 
processes is altering the speed, depth and confidence with 
which dealmakers assess risk and opportunity. In a 
landscape where regulatory and economic assumptions can 
change rapidly, modeling capability and execution readiness 
are becoming central to sustained performance.
This Global M&A Outlook examines how these forces are 
converging. Drawing on global survey data and practitioner 
insight, it shows how the sources of advantage in M&A are 
evolving — and why execution capability is emerging as a 
durable institutional asset in an increasingly complex deal 
environment.
Foreword
Professor Scott Moeller
Founder, M&A Research Centre
Bayes Business School
City St George’s, University of London

Executive summary
Deal activity regained momentum through 2025 and survey 
findings indicate that many organizations expect pipelines to 
expand further in 2026. Yet this recovery is unfolding in a 
structurally more complex environment. Legislative and 
regulatory volatility, evolving trade regimes and 
transformational changes in global tax frameworks are 
reshaping forward-looking cost structures and return profiles.
In this context, valuation discussions are increasingly defined 
not by headline multiples alone, but by alignment of buyer and 
seller expectations amid shifting assumptions. When effective 
tax rates, supply chain economics and regulatory thresholds 
are moving targets, pricing certainty becomes harder to 
establish — and execution readiness becomes more 
important.
Against this backdrop, carve-outs are emerging as a central 
mechanism for portfolio reshaping, positioning 2026 as the 
year of the carve-out.
A multi-speed global market, led by the US
Deal momentum is strengthening globally, but unevenly. US-
based organizations report higher confidence, stronger 
pipelines and greater readiness to transact. Outside the US 
dealmakers face a more complex mix of macroeconomic, 
regulatory and geopolitical conditions.
Rather than dampening activity, this divergence is sharpening 
competitive dynamics. Organizations are prioritizing 
transactions that reinforce strategic coherence and can be 
executed with discipline in a volatile environment.
Diverging risk appetites reshaping competition 
for assets
Private equity firms and corporate acquirers are approaching 
2026 with different mandates and execution infrastructure. 
Private equity firms report higher expectations for pipeline 
growth, supported by capital deployment imperatives, 
improving financing conditions and the gradual reopening of 
exit markets. Corporate portfolio reshaping is also bringing 
additional assets to market through separations. Corporates, 
while active, are balancing M&A against broader enterprise 
transformation priorities and integration capacity.
Global M&A momentum is rebuilding, but the foundations of the market have shifted in ways that will likely reshape how deals are executed and where 
value is created
